record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures reasoning-benchmark performance against response length and compares two model sizes, but does not use the original held-out cross-entropy scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining loss or sweep parameter count, training tokens, or training compute to fit the claimed pretraining power laws or compute-optimal allocation. It reports separate test-time response-length scaling results in Figures 6 and 8, which bear on V6. Main benchmark tables compare model scores but do not report scaling curves; cited scaling-law findings are not the paper's own results.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only as motivation. Its own scaling results concern RL-trained reasoning accuracy against mean response length, a test-time and RL axis. It also compares two unnamed model sizes, with no parameter counts, no pretraining loss, and no curve over parameters, tokens or training compute. None of this measures what V1–V7 name. V6 is about downstream gains with pretraining scale or loss, not with chain-of-thought length.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that scaling context length is crucial to continued improvement of LLMs trained with RL. They add that larger models are more token-efficient, while smaller models with longer CoTs can reach comparable performance under a test-time budget. They also claim strong results without MCTS, value functions or process reward models, and that long2short methods improve short-CoT models.
record.recipe_differences: Measures RL reasoning-benchmark performance against response length and compares model sizes; does not fit held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with response length and model size; the paper reports the larger model is generally more token-efficient and the smaller model can catch up with longer CoTs.

fits_no_version.finding: For an internal mid-sized model, accuracy on eight reasoning benchmarks rises roughly linearly with mean response length during RL (Fig. 6 trend slopes 1.36e-05 to 4.24e-05 per token).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning accuracy rises steadily with chain-of-thought length learned through RL (test-time/RL length scaling).

fits_no_version.finding: A larger model starts higher and is more token-efficient. A smaller model reaches comparable accuracy with longer RL-trained CoTs (Fig. 8; sizes unstated).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model size and RL-trained response length trade off in reasoning performance.

record.problems: The Figure 6 and Figure 8 results are presented as plots without numeric benchmark accuracies in the text. Model parameter counts are not stated. The paper's explicit scaling-law measurements concern response length/test-time computation, not held-out pretraining loss or training compute.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Figures 1–3 and Tables 2–3 benchmark comparisons because they report isolated model benchmark scores rather than performance scaling curves. Omitted Figure 5 training-iteration trajectories and Figures 9–10 sampling/policy-optimization ablations because they do not test the claim versions recorded here.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits over parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape comparison at fixed parameters. Appendix B.3 defers architecture scaling experiments to future work.
No power-law loss fits in other modalities or regimes.
No downstream performance against pretraining parameters, tokens, compute or loss. The two-size comparison has unstated sizes and no curve over scale.
No analysis of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V6 verdicts is overturned. V6 concerns downstream gains with pretraining scale or loss, while this paper's 'scaling' is RL response length. The Fig. 8 size comparison has unnamed sizes and only two points. Appendix B.3 asserts unreported scaling experiments showing data quality dominates base-model performance, with no numbers. All rows are reclassified under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or power-law fits over parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
No prediction of larger-run pretraining loss from fits on smaller runs.
No fixed training-compute budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law loss forms across modalities or training regimes.

The paper examines benchmark performance against response length/test-time computation and compares two model sizes; it does not test performance against pretraining loss or establish predictable downstream performance from pretraining parameter, token, or compute scaling.
No analysis of fitting choices or exponents for the cited pretraining scaling laws, or of disagreement between such laws.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Internal long-CoT model; benchmark performance versus mean response length in Figure 6
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a strong correlation between output context length and problem-solving capability, with positive trend slopes shown for the eight benchmarks (F6-omni through F6-kaoyan).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Two model sizes across four reasoning benchmarks in Figure 8
reader_labels.reason: The larger model initially performs better and is generally more token-efficient, but the smaller model can reach comparable performance with longer CoTs; parameter counts and numeric plotted accuracies are not stated (F8-omni-small through F8-aime-large).
